text:
Court of Queen
’
s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Karmel
v Calgary Jewish Academy, 2015 ABQB 731

Date:
20151120

Docket:
1301 05064

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

Benjamin Karmel

Plaintiff

- and -

Calgary Jewish Academy

Defendant

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of the

Honourable
Mr. Justice

A.D. Macleod

_______________________________________________________

Introduction and
Issues

[
1
]

The Calgary Jewish Academy (CJA) terminated its
Principal, Mr. Karmel, on February 25, 2013 for cause. The reasons that the CJA
argues amount to cause are listed in Appendix A to the Notice of Termination.
They relate to issues of enrollment, the grade 4 class, the IPP process,
communication style, the principal improvement plan, and technology. Other
miscellaneous concerns include denial of enrollment for children in August 2012,
unprofessional behavior by staff, the teachers’ websites, not conducting exit
interviews, scheduling personal vacation time, and the choice of paint colors
for the school hallways. In other words, it relies on a wide range of causes.

[
2
]

Mr. Karmel was hired by the CJA while he was the
head of school at the Richmond Jewish Day School in British Columbia. He was
hired for a five-year term commencing August 1, 2006. On November 26, 2010, the
CJA renewed his contract for another five-year term commencing September 1,
2011. The agreement provided that the CJA could terminate Mr. Karmel for cause
prior to the expiry of the contract, and the reasons for termination were to be
in writing. The main issue before me is whether the CJA had just cause to
terminate the contract. If not, is Mr. Karmel entitled to punitive, exemplary
or other damages in addition to that owing to him under the contract?

[
3
]

The trial commenced November 24, 2014, and
continued through that week and the following week. Argument concluded on
December 19, 2014.

[
4
]

The parties agreed that the CJA would call its
case first. Its witnesses included a number of its Board members including Adam
Brener, Dr. Joshua Benjamin, Mr. Eric Kettner, Stan Eisenberg and Aviva Horwitz,
as well as Audrey Goldfarb and Yossi Suissa.

[
5
]

In addition to Mr. Karmel, the Plaintiff called
Ms. Karmel, Ms. Bondar, and Ms. Halpern.

[
6
]

Many documents were entered, most notably four
binders of documents, Exhibits 14-17, which were consecutively tabbed. I will
refer to those documents by referencing the tab number. There were other
exhibits as well, including an Agreed Statement of Facts marked Exhibit 3.

[
7
]

It was CJA policy to evaluate its Director, Head
of School or Principal, as Mr. Karmel was variously called, on a regular basis.
A review was done in May of 2008 and there was another scheduled for the summer
of 2011.

[
8
]

Audrey Goldfarb of Minnesota conducted the
latter evaluation. It is important to understand that the evaluation process
was intended to be a two way street. It was a collaborative process in which
the Principal and the executive or Board were to communicate and explore ways
to improve the effectiveness of the Principal. The ultimate goal was to help
make the school stronger. As Ms. Goldfarb testified, this could not have been
achieved from the “top down.” In order for the evaluation to be effective, it
had to be a collaborative effort. She would not have done the evaluation if the
Board had insisted on a “top down” approach. Furthermore, Ms. Goldfarb emphasized
that the ongoing improvement plan established for the Principal had to be a
collaborative effort as well. The intention was to maximize the opportunity for
growth on the part of the Principal.

[
9
]

The fact that the evaluation process was not
part of Mr. Karmel’s contract renewal emphasizes that the intent was to improve
the Principal’s effectiveness rather than to assess his suitability. Ms.
Goldfarb also confirmed that it was important for the school to work
continuously on its strategic plan. It was necessary that the school define
itself in terms of its students and the Calgary Jewish community it serves.

[
10
]

The 2008 evaluation of Mr. Karmel was
complimentary. Mr. Karmel is well qualified and has an excellent background. By
all accounts, he has always worked incredibly hard and was dedicated to the
CJA. Indeed, the 2008 evaluation expressed concern about the possibility of
burn out. It also emphasized the importance of preserving the Principal’s time
for leadership within the school, and to free up the Principal as much as
possible from more mundane tasks. The 2008 evaluation also recognized that the
parents of the school were often opinionated and sometimes difficult to deal
with. My review of the evidence and testimony given at this trial confirms that
observation. I also note that this became more acute in the final two years of
Mr. Karmel’s tenure.

[
11
]

The CJA is a day school that serves preschool to
grade nine. In addition to an excellent academic education, the CJA also offers
a traditional Jewish education.

[
12
]

Historically the school has faced many
challenges, including reduced enrollment. Education for children in Calgary has
become very competitive. Not surprisingly, the CJA faces stiff competition from
other private schools in the city, as well as public schools. CJA students go
elsewhere for high school and often, prior to that, parents will put their
children in alternative schools if they feel it will better prepare them for high
school studies. For that reason, the CJA has had an Attraction and Retention
Committee for several years.

[
13
]

As in many schools, an elected Board of
volunteers oversees the CJA. The Board then elects one of their number as
President for a two-year term. The Principal reports directly to the Board.  It
is essential to the school’s success to have a good working relationship
between the Board and the Principal. The Principal attends all the Board
meetings and usually submits a comprehensive report at every meeting. It is my
observation from the evidence that, in the absence of a healthy relationship
between the Board and the Principal, the school ceases to function effectively.
The morale of the staff, Principal, students and parents declines. From the
fall of 2011 to Mr. Karmel’s termination in February 2013, it would be a gross
understatement to say that the Principal and the President of the CJA did not
see eye to eye. The relationship between the Board and its Principal became intolerable,
and the morale of the CJA rapidly deteriorated.

Onus of Proof

[
14
]

The CJA must prove on a balance of probabilities
that it had just cause to terminate Mr. Karmel without notice for disobeying the
directions of the Board. The following paragraph from
Port Arthur
Shipbuilding v Arthurs
,
1967 CanLII 30 (ON CA)
, [1967] 2 OR 49, OJ 972 (Ont CA) at para
11
is a
helpful passage on this subject:

If an a employee has been guilty of
misconduct, habitual neglect of duty, incompetence, or conduct incompatible
with his duties, or prejudicial to the employer’s business, or if he has been
guilty of willful disobedience to the employer’s orders in a matter of
substance, the law recognizes the employer’s right to summarily dismiss the
delinquent employee.

Is Just
Cause Established?

[
15
]

The CJA argues that Mr. Karmel was wilfully
disobedient in the face of reasonable demands by the Board on matters of
importance. Accordingly, the CJA argues that just cause has been made out.

[
16
]

Howard A. Levitt in
The Law of Dismissal in
Canada
, 2d ed. (Aurora: Canada Law Book, 1992) defines wilful disobedience
as defiance by an employee of a lawful and reasonable order that effectively repudiates
the essential condition of the employment relationship; that employees must
obey their employer's instruction. Levitt goes on to set out ten elements
required for insubordination to constitute just cause for dismissal:

1.

the order must be either clear and specific or
must be a breach of policies and procedures well known by the employee;

2.

the order must be within the scope of the
employee’s job duties;

3.

the order must be reasonable and lawful;

4.

the disobedience must be both deliberate and
intentional rather than resulting from an honest mistake as to whether the
order was still in effect or under the reasonable belief that he was not
contravening orders;

5.

the order must involve some matter of
importance;

6.

unless the act of disobedience is particularly
serious it has to be repeated, rather than be an isolated act of disobedience,
in order to constitute cause;

7.

it must be shown that as a result of the
disobedience the relationship was so damaged that it could not be carried on;

8.

it must be shown that the employee understood or
should have understood that he ran the risk of being terminated for
disregarding the order;

9.

if there is a reasonable explanation for the
disobedience it will not be cause for discharge; and

10.

there will be more latitude shown to long-service employees.

Levitt’s principles were endorsed by this Court in
Wilson v KP
Manufacturers (Calgary) Ltd
,

1998 CanLII 18141 (AB QB)
, 1998 225 AR 205, 60 Alta LR (3d) 333 (Alta QB) at paras
10-11
.

[
17
]

In order for wilful disobedience to be just
cause for termination, the employee’s behaviour must be “seriously incompatible
with the employee's duties... conduct which goes to the root of the contract
and fundamentally strikes at the employment relationship”: see
Panton v
Everywoman’s Health Centre Society

(1988)
,
2000 BCCA 621
, BCLR
(3d) 364 at para
28
.

[
18
]

Insubordination will constitute cause where the
employer can establish that the employee wilfully violates a “clear and
unequivocal” instruction or refuses “to carry out a policy or procedure well
known by the employee to be central to the fulfilment of the employer’s
objectives”: see
Panton

at para
33
.

[
19
]

For the reasons that follow, I find that Mr.
Karmel was in no way wilfully disobedient. The evidence does not establish disobedience
or insubordination; rather it demonstrates a lack of good faith on the part of
the CJA. Just cause is therefore not made out and Mr. Karmel is entitled to
damages.

Narrative
and Findings of Fact

[
20
]

The main protagonists in this case are the
Plaintiff, Mr. Benjamin Karmel, and the President and Chair of the Board, Mr. Eric
Kettner. They both gave evidence. Mr. Karmel impressed me at as a truthful
witness. At the time of the trial, he was 61 years of age and had a long
history as an educator. He received a Master’s in Education from the University
of Calgary, and from 1993 to 2002 he taught at the CJA. He then became Head of
School at the Richmond Jewish Day School in British Columbia until he returned
to the CJA as Principal. Mr. Karmel impressed me as being totally dedicated to
the CJA and a very hard worker. He had definite ideas on many of the issues
facing the school, and my assessment of him as a witness is in line with the
comments of Mr. Burghardt, who had prepared the complimentary 2008 evaluation.

[
21
]

Mr. Karmel knew the school and the issues facing
it and had many sound ideas on how to manage those issues. Diplomatic talents
were not his forte and he occasionally rubbed people the wrong way.
Nevertheless, no one ever questioned his dedication to the CJA, his hard work
or his qualifications to do the job. Moreover, he impressed me as a man of
great integrity. But for this termination, I think he would have finished his
career as an educator at a high level.

[
22
]

Mr. Kettner is an experienced businessman with a
Bachelor of Commerce Degree. He was first involved at the CJA in 2010-2011
school year as Treasurer, and became Chairman of the Board in the summer of
2011. He had no prior experience in running a school, nor did he have any prior
board experience. Of the fourteen members of the Board, five were new at the
beginning of Mr. Kettner’s first term as Chairman and President.

[
23
]

Mr. Kettner impressed me as inflexible and
controlling. He insisted upon a hierarchical structure of which he was the
head. He likened the school to a corporation, and his role to that of a Chief
Executive Officer. This may work well in a commercial setting. It did not,
however, work well at the CJA, where the Board is made up of volunteer members
who must rely upon the Principal and the rest of the administration for their
expertise in education.  Furthermore, Mr. Kettner took parents’ complaints very
seriously, and as a criticism of Mr. Karmel and his staff. He often took the
parents’ side on issues and he invariably supported the Board parents when they
had issues with Mr. Karmel or his staff.

[
24
]

While the Principal reported to the Board, it is
important that the Board benefit from the Principal’s experience and understand
the Principal’s point of view on issues facing the school. In Mr. Karmel’s
prior experience, that was the norm.

i.

August 2011

[
25
]

While there is no evidence that Mr. Kettner and
Mr. Karmel had any negative interaction prior to August 2011, on August 16
there was an unfortunate and, in my view, bizarre encounter between Mr. Karmel
and Mr. Kettner. Mr. Kettner had not sought a meeting to discuss the CJA’s
issues with Mr. Karmel prior to that time.

[
26
]

Mr. Kettner called Mr. Karmel on August 16 and
told him that some parents had expressed concerns regarding paint colours in
the school hallways. Mr. Kettner was worried about the painting process. Mr.
Karmel responded that this was not his area and that he would connect Mr.
Kettner with the Building Superintendent and the Custodian who were responsible,
so that Mr. Kettner could find out more about the process.

[
27
]

While Mr. Kettner did meet with the
Superintendent and Custodian on August 16, he later complained to Mr. Karmel
that there was no need for Mr. Kettner to be at a meeting with them, and that
he wanted to meet with the Principal and not with his staff. For reasons that I
still cannot comprehend, there ensued an argument in which Mr. Karmel made the
point that paint color was not part of his job nor was it Mr. Kettner’s responsibility.
Tempers escalated and Mr. Kettner demanded of Mr. Karmel two or three times to
stop speaking. He told him this was an example of his communication issues. Mr.
Kettner claimed that Mr. Karmel then threatened to resign, to which Mr. Kettner
replied, “if you put it in writing I will accept your resignation.” Mr.
Karmel’s version was that he said, “Are you trying to get me to resign?” He
denies that he threatened to resign. I accept Mr. Karmel’s recollection of this
event. Wherever Mr. Karmel’s evidence conflicts with that of Mr. Kettner, I accept
the evidence of Mr. Karmel.

[
28
]

Mr. Kettner concedes that he lost his temper and
had to cool off for some 30 minutes. This incident appears to have had a
lasting effect on the relationship between Mr. Kettner and Mr. Karmel. I find
Mr. Kettner’s behavior in this petty situation to be astonishing. Mr. Karmel’s
explanation that he left the paint colour decisions to others was perfectly
normal and understandable. His attempt to put those in charge of paint in touch
with Mr. Kettner was also understandable. Mr. Kettner’s reaction, however, was
not.

[
29
]

Prior to the August 16 incident, a call with Ms.
Goldfarb had been scheduled for August 17. Ms. Goldfarb was conducting the 2011
Principal evaluation. Most, if not all, of the previous conversations with Ms.
Goldfarb were done in the presence of Mr. Karmel. On this day, however, the
telephone conversation did not include him. During the call, Mr. Kettner
informed the participants that Mr. Karmel had threatened to resign over the
paint colour issue. At this time, Ms. Goldfarb was told that Mr. Karmel had
threatened to resign even though he had not. Faced with this news, Ms. Goldfarb
suggested that Mr. Kettner might wish to consult an employment lawyer. Mr.
Kettner contacted a lawyer that same day.

[
30
]

Two days later Ms. Horwitz, another Board member,
and Mr. Kettner met with Mr. Karmel. This August 19 conversation was recorded
without Mr. Karmel’s knowledge. Tab 32 is a series of talking points by Mr.
Kettner, as well as his rendition of the conversation between himself, Ms.
Horwitz and Mr. Karmel. The evidence discloses that Mr. Kettner was successful
in recruiting Ms. Horowitz to his position with regard to Mr. Karmel.

i.

2011-2012 School Year

[
31
]

Tab 43 is a copy of Mr. Karmel’s state of the
School address on September 22, 2011. In this address he thoughtfully, in my
view, reviews his ideas on enrollment, the budget, the climate of the learning
community culture, analysis of the Fraser Institute Reports, and other matters
relating to the CJA.

[
32
]

Following the address he asked the Board for
feedback with respect to the new Ambassador Program. On October 1 he wrote
directly to all of the executive members, enclosing a number of academic
materials on various educational issues of general interest. In an email to Mr.
Karmel of October 6, 2011, at Tab 66, Mr. Kettner expressed concern about Mr.
Karmel damaging the effectiveness of “my leadership and Board morale.” Mr.
Kettner went on to say

As I’ve
stated to you previously, if there are any concerns about the Board as a whole
they are to come to me directly and never to the Board as a whole until I have
had a chance to reflect on them and bring them to the Board myself. Your email
to the Board members (after I asked you to take no further action) saying there
is a group of Ambassadors that question their transparency,  credibility and
invisibility is a direct attack on my authority by [sic] Administration and
cannot happen in the future.

[
33
]

There was clearly a clash in philosophy. Mr.
Karmel believed that criticism should be shared openly among those concerned
with the CJA’s governance. Mr. Kettner, on the other hand, espoused solidarity
and, as Chair, wished to control the flow of information to Board members.

[
34
]

Unbeknownst to Mr. Karmel, an “in camera”
meeting of the Board had been scheduled for October 11, 2011, to deal with the
report of the Principal Evaluation Committee (PEC). This meeting also appointed
an ad hoc committee of the Board to take over the monitoring of the Principal
Improvement Plan (PIP). Mr. Karmel became aware of the “in camera” meeting and was
alarmed. These meetings are closed or private sessions with no recorded
minutes. It was Mr. Karmel’s experience that boards almost never called an “in
camera” meeting unless it concerned contract negotiations. In his experience, boards
were always quick to reassure him when they did have private meetings that
there were of no concern to him or his role as Principal. Mr. Karmel was
understandably worried that members of the Board would be taking decisions on
the PEC and PIP without receiving all of the facts and arguments.

[
35
]

As a result, Mr. Karmel sent each member of the
Board a memo (Tab 71), a response to  Mr. Kettner’s October 6 email. While the
memo is lengthy, Mr. Karmel expressed his concerns about the lack of
transparent governance and the control by the Chair of the information flow to the
Board on issues of school governance. Mr. Karmel felt that he had been set up
to fail, and thought it was important for the Board to understand his point of
view. He also felt, apparently wrongly, that the Board wished to know his point
of view on these matters.

[
36
]

The memo to the Board brought about a swift
reaction

from Mr. Kettner, who emailed Mr. Karmel on October 7 and copied
the Vice Chairs; see Tab 75. The email included the following paragraph:

Again you
have gone directly to the Executive with your concerns about them when I’ve
specifically asked you at least twice to not do this again. This is not at all
appropriate and undermines my authority. I welcome any concerns you have and
will bring them to the Executive myself whether they relate to the Board as a
whole or to me individually.  I ask that you immediately cease any sort of
direct communication with the Executive that relates to how the Executive
should operate and how the President should do his job.

[
37
]

Under previous Chairs, Mr. Karmel testified that
he would be consulted on all matters related to the Board’s agendas, and he had
never before been told that he was unable to communicate directly with Board
members.

[
38
]

Mr. Karmel and Mr. Kettner were off on a bad
footing, and Mr. Kettner had consulted legal counsel. While that consultation
is privileged, Mr. Kettner would no doubt have been told that Mr. Karmel had a five-year
contract that could only be terminated with just cause.

[
39
]

Attached to Exhibit 9 is a bill rendered by a
law firm to the CJA. A consultation occurred on “strategy and options” on
August 17, 2011. The bill also references “process” and “drafting resolution
regarding mandate”. I have no doubt this refers to the mandate received by the
PEC at the “in camera” meeting on October 11, 2011. Further, following
consultation with counsel, communication between Mr. Kettner and Mr. Karmel was
mostly in writing.

[
40
]

I note that there are no minutes of the above
mentioned “in camera” meeting of October 11, but we have Mr. Kettner’s speaking
notes at Tabs 79 and 283. The views expressed at Tab 283 are candid and
represent Mr. Kettner’s real opinion. I have little doubt that he shared his
opinion with the Board. I find that these speaking notes account for much of
what Mr. Kettner communicated to the Board at the meeting. He delivered the
remarks under a warning of confidentiality, and they contained insidious
criticism of Mr. Karmel. Mr. Kettner’s comments overall were unmeasured and
unbalanced. The process as a whole was extremely unfair.

[
41
]

As a result of the “in camera” meeting, the
Board reconstituted the PEC. Mr. Kettner was named as Chair, and the committee
included Adam Brener and Stan Eisenberg. Clearly, the message to the Board was
that the PEC was necessary to rein in Mr. Karmel, who was going in the wrong
direction and refused to be managed by CJA’s Board. Thus, Mr. Kettner was
actively pitting the Board against the Principal and utilizing an “in camera”
confidential meeting to recruit the Board to his point of view. In my view, he
was not acting in good faith. Further, on October 11, the same day as the “in
camera” meeting, Ms. Horwitz, Vice President, sent a letter to Mr. Karmel on
behalf of the Board. The letter directed that all future communication be sent
exclusively to the Board’s President, Mr. Kettner. The letter made clear that
the Board was unanimously behind Mr. Kettner. From that point forward, it was clear
that there was to be no partnership in education; a chasm existed between Mr.
Karmel and the Board.

[
42
]

The agreed exhibits include numerous notes made
by Mr. Kettner, as well as memos to members of the Board. These are
uncomplimentary to Mr. Karmel and further demonstrate Mr. Kettner’s contempt of
him. Tab138 is a March 28, 2012 email, one of many to colleagues on the PEC
containing derogatory comments about Mr. Karmel. This particular email references
“24 hours with Biff”. Biff is a character from the play “Death of a Salesman”
by Arthur Miller, and it was not meant as a complimentary label. Moreover, the
fact that Mr. Kettner felt free to refer to the Principal as “Biff” when
corresponding with professional colleagues speaks volumes.

[
43
]

Tab 124 is another example of an email in which Mr.
Kettner rants about Mr. Karmel; this time to Tracey Forman, a Board member and
former Chair. He complains about Mr. Karmel’s incompetence, and compares his
ability to be Principal at CJA to Mr. Kettner’s own ability to coach the
Calgary Flames.

[
44
]

It is Ms. Forman’s earlier email to Mr. Kettner,
also at Tab 124, which is ultimately more revealing. Her email is dated March
1, 2012, and it includes the following:

...I find it interesting that executive has felt compelled to
“micro-manage” administration over the last few years more than ever. In those
years we have also seen marked exodus from the school. Yet... we never really
did stop and ask ourselves if maybe the additional involvement and demands the
executive placed on Ben/Administration could be the reason for the exodus-
maybe our non- professional opinions on what needed to happen, have steered us
wrong.- or at the very least, taken Ben’s focus away from what he ( as a
professional educator) thinks he should be doing.

It’s kind of a devil’s advocate question... but hearing Rory
Paul’s rant made me think... if nothing else, we have been guilty of NOT
trusting the “professional educators” of our school. Us doubting Ben is really
NOT good for anyone. I believe it has frustrated Ben and it has demoralized the
executive. I personally cannot take another “negative Ben bashing” meeting.

Eric... you & I alone, are likely the only ones who see
how hard, and how long Ben works for our school. It’s not that he doesn’t have
some serious flaws (who of us doesn’t), and that he hasn’t made some mistakes
(again who of us hasn’t), but he is still at our school, and still WANTS to be
at our school in spite of all the s#^! He has to deal with from some very
overbearing (not always reasonable) parents. Plus an executive that doesn’t
believe in him. I couldn’t take it.

Ben has welcomed CAIS, he welcomed the CTBS and HE was the
one who stated that as a community school we needed to be able to educate the
gifted and the special needs too. That was NEVER Claude’s philosophy- that was
all Ben.

I know I am the only cheerleader for Ben. It’s my greatest
flaw (or perhaps strength) to see the good in people, to see their potential.
The group that hired Ben, the group that voted to renew his contract saw these
things too. I believe that we are headed in the right direction by looking at
the things he is not good at, and getting them off his plate. I also believe
that a knowledgeable communications person would be worth every penny.

[
45
]

This memo is consistent with the evidence before
me that the Board, through Mr. Kettner, was micro managing Mr. Karmel. As Ms.
Forman underscored, no one on the Board had qualifications to rival Mr.
Karmel’s as an educator. The email also confirms that many meetings of the
executive ended up as a negative “Ben bashing” meetings. At this point, and for
little or no reason, the Chair, the PEC and likely much of the Board, had no
confidence in Mr. Karmel. This view of the Principal was the result of a
process that was unfair and unbalanced. Furthermore, it was all done under the
cloak of confidentiality. The only knowledge Mr. Karmel had of any of this was
based upon rumour or suspicion. Unhappily, Ms. Forman’s email was but one voice
in what should have been a chorus. However, most Board members did not have Ms.
Forman’s experience and they had been influenced and unfairly prejudiced against
the Principal by Mr. Kettner.

[
46
]

A meeting between the PEC and Mr. Karmel was
held on March 28, 2012. At Tab 141 are Mr. Kettner’s talking points, which convey
the message communicated to Mr. Karmel at this meeting.

[
47
]

Following the meeting, Mr. Karmel responded to
Mr. Kettner (Tab 142). It is interesting to contrast tabs 141 and 142. Mr.
Kettner clearly viewed the PEC and the PIP differently from Mr. Karmel. The PEC
viewed its role as establishing criteria against which the Principal was to be
measured. Mr. Karmel, in contrast, continued to believe that the PIP was a
collaborative process. It was meant to be implemented in good faith, with
positive benefits to both the school and the Principal. I find that a process
of good faith and collaboration was the proper and original intention of the
PIP.  The process adopted, however was, not in line with this approach. Rather
it proceeded to document the PEC’s dissatisfaction with Mr. Karmel.

ii.

2012-2013 School Year

[
48
]

The 2012-2013 school year began with the Board
Orientation meeting. This was an annual event, particularly aimed at new
members. In 2012 there were another five new members on the Board. In previous
years, the Orientation meeting invariably included the Principal. In September
2012, however, the Board held the meeting without Mr. Karmel, despite him
usually being a key figure. Understandably, Mr. Karmel was confused and hurt.
We have the benefit of Mr. Kettner’s speaking notes at Tab 182. He informed the
meeting’s participants that enrollment had declined since Mr. Karmel’s contract
was renewed. He also told them that there had been a loss of confidence in Mr.
Karmel’s leadership. While that represented Mr. Kettner’s own view, it was most
unfair of him to share with the others this negative perception, particularly
at the first meeting of the school year.

[
49
]

Mr. Kettner further advised the Board at this
meeting that the CJA had sought legal advice, and that Mr. Karmel had a “no cut”
contract. The CJA would have to pay him the balance in order to terminate him. Mr.
Kettner informed the Board that this was not financially viable.

[
50
]

At Tab 189 there is an email dated September 20,
2012, from Mr. Kettner to Mr. Brener, Mr. Eisenberg and Mr. Benjamin on the
subject of “I like sharing my joy”. It was another “Ben bashing” memo which
concluded as follows:

I am still not sure on how to respond. Stan’s earlier
suggestion to me to just tell Ben to take care of this mess appropriately makes
the most sense, but I wonder, too, if there’s a way to use it against him. I’m
looking for some more suggestions.

[
51
]

This email is evidence that the PEC was not
working to improve the situation. Rather Mr. Kettner was looking for a way to
sabotage Mr. Karmel, and he was not the least bit shy about sharing that intention
with the email recipients.  That he was doing so, and seeking the assistance of
others (there is no response in evidence), suggests that the recipients were
not offended by the notion of plotting against Mr. Karmel. I find that the PEC was
not conducting its mandate in good faith. Mr. Kettner was controlling the flow
of information to the other members of the committee, and had succeeded in
recruiting them to his point of view. The other volunteer members did not
challenge Mr. Kettner or his views. It was clear from their evidence at trial
that the PEC members were aligned with Mr. Kettner’s opinion of the Principal.

[
52
]

To put matters in perspective, the CJA, despite
its difficulties, was achieving academically. Some of its accomplishments are included
in the “Principal’s Perspective” at Tab 167. The school did well in the Fraser
rankings, and was accepted as a candidate by the Canadian Accredited
Independent Schools (CAIS); at the time, there were only four private schools
in Calgary that were CAIS accredited.

[
53
]

At Tab 198 is a document entitled “Ratification
of the mandate of the Special Committee- October 10, 2012”. Apparently this was
a motion that was passed by the Board at its meeting October 10, 2012, although
the minutes exhibited at the trial do not contain a record of this motion. It
may well be that this was another “in camera” session. According to Mr. Karmel,
these sessions were increasingly common at the end of regular Board meetings.
In any event, this motion devolved the role of evaluating the Principal on the
Board’s behalf to the PEC. It also provided the PEC with the power necessary to
carry out this mandate. By this point, if not earlier, I find that Mr. Kettner
was determined to terminate Mr. Karmel.

[
54
]

No one informed Mr. Karmel of this new mandate. He
had, however, heard a rumor that the Board was out to get him. A female Board
member had apparently shared this with another parent, and it found its way to
Mr. Karmel. This was understandably upsetting to Mr. Karmel, and he wrote a
long letter to the PEC dated October 28, 2012 (Tab 204). The letter contains a
litany of concerns, and was clearly written by someone who felt isolated and
under attack. Mr. Karmel referred to the Board as micro managing the School. He
discussed the divisive atmosphere and the hostility between the Board and the administration.
He itemized many examples of Board behavior that he believed had contributed to
the climate of workplace hostility, and pleaded with the Board to take his
concerns seriously. He concluded as follows:

Despite the concerns I’ve outlined above, I continue to have
faith in all of us. It is time for us to move together within an environment
with humility, positive communication and mutual high regard and strategic
direction. Anything less is unbecoming for the CJA. I am continuing with the
hard work ahead and will work in good faith with the Board. I expect the same
in return.

[
55
]

If that was his expectation it was ill founded. Mr.
Kettner was determined to vacate Mr. Karmel from his position as Principal of
the CJA.

[
56
]

A meeting between the PEC and Mr. Karmel took
place on October 29, 2012. Mr. Josh Benjamin, who was not a member of the
committee, joined the meeting. It was recorded at Mr. Karmel’s request. As had
become common with other CJA executive meetings, there was little notice and no
agenda. The committee presented Mr. Karmel with a letter on their behalf. The letter,
dated October 29, 2012, became the subject matter of subsequent correspondence.
It was also referred to in much of the evidence given at trial. For this reason
I set the content of the letter out in its entirety:

Mr. Ben Karmel

Principal

Calgary Jewish
Academy

October 29, 2012

Dear Ben,

Our committee has
been working with you, as leader of the CJA, for the past year to help you in
your role as Principal. In light of the Board’s fiduciary responsibilities to

of concern for the CJA and the direction it is headed under your leadership in

We had intended to bring this letter to you in early September, but out of
respect to you and in consideration of your personal matters early in that
month, we postponed its delivery until now.

As you are aware,
more than 100 students have left the CJA for other schools over the past three

our reserve funds are being depleted as the school faces a budget deficit for
the third time in four years.

In reviewing your
Personal Improvement Plan and the standards expected of a principal in Alberta

Guideline (February, 2009), we have identified problems that have hindered both

find the problems that require your immediate attention:

1)

Professionalism- As a private school, with
significantly tuition fees, parents have an expectation of excellence. Some
recent examples indicating a marked departure from the expected standard of
professionalism:

•

Numerous communications
to parents with spelling and grammatical errors.

•

Administration and
staff have been disrespectful in communications with parents and board members
at the school, including Mrs. Horwitz, Mrs. Cheuk, and Mrs. Barkai.

•

Some CJA staff members
have been sending emails to parents on Shabbat and Jewish Holidays

•

Failure by you to reply
to email correspondence and meeting requests

•

The handling of the
situation with the foster children that arose prior to the start of the
2012-2013 school year. Initially you would not enrol the children as you felt

that JFS decided that it would be best for these children to attend Akiva
Academy. However, JFS has maintained, throughout, the children’s best interests
would be served by attending the CJA.

For the CJA to
succeed in becoming, once again, a well-respected and financially sustainable

the CJA’s activities, inside and outside the school. WE require a draft action

2)

Technology integration- Within the CJA
Mission statement, as well as the Principle Quality Practice Guideline, the

(teacher laptops were also purchased). The problems brought to you on previous
occasions continue, including:

•

Under-utilization of
classroom monitors. Most teachers use them sparingly, if at all.

•

The Board is not aware
of teachers creating “Khan Academy” like video segments which were highlighted
when the proposal was presented.

•

Reweb was to be fully
implemented over 13 months ago.

•

There are
inconsistencies between teachers and grades regarding the use of Renweb for

To help ensure the
success of these programs, we required detailed reports on both the Renweb and

3)

Personal Improvement Plan- The Personal
Improvement Plan (“PIP”) was developed by you and the consultant, Audrey
Goldfarb, to assist in improving your leadership skills and introduce various
strategies to improve the school and its reputation. This PIP was agreed to,
and accepted by, you and the Board. The Committee extended you much latitude
for compliance with the target class. As neither the enrolment nor the
financial picture of the school has improved, there is no longer room for
leeway. While all the PIP items are important, the Board has prioritized the
following outstanding items as the Board feels these are crucial for the CJA at
this time:

a.

Leadership #1- Develop
teachers as leaders. Engaged staff in focus areas of inquiry.

b.

Leadership #4- Develop
a plan to increase enrolment.

c.

Education Excellence
#1- Clarify methods of measuring school achievement and success.

d.

Educational Excellence
#2- Enrich Curriculum to meet school values and achievement goals.

e.

Wider Community Perception- Principal and
Admissions Director will develop an annual schedule to increase opportunities
to speak and feature school in the wider community.

Several of these
are long past due; others (items “a” and “d”) are ongoing responsibilities. We
require reports on the progress of these items on a weekly basis. The deadline
for completions of items “b”, “c”, and “e” is December 28
th
, 2012.

Ben, we have
identified and brought these problems to you for your own benefit. Ultimately,
our goals in this are for you to succeed as principal of the CJA and for the
school to be set on a course toward another 100 years of success. Please come
to us if you require any additional support or resources to accomplish these
goals so we can do our best to meet your needs to enable you to succeed.

[
57
]

I am sure that Mr. Kettner wrote the final
passage, and I am equally sure that he did not wish for Mr. Karmel’s success.
The letter is yet another example of bad faith dealings on the part of the PEC
and Mr. Kettner.

[
58
]

Prior to this October 29, 2012 meeting, the PEC
had not met with Mr. Karmel since April of that year. At that time there had
been general discussion of the successes and failures of the Principal as
perceived by the committee. Mr. Karmel had made extensive responses to those
issues; see Tabs 142, 143, 144 and 146. Yet Mr. Karmel did not receive a reply
to these efforts from the PEC. Mr. Karmel had also invited collaborative
discussion between the committee and himself, but none occurred. Instead, the
next thing Mr. Karmel received was the letter set out in above.

[
59
]

Given the way things were left between the PEC
and Mr. Karmel in April 2012, the letter of October 29 could not have come as anything
but a surprise to Mr. Karmel. The PEC was not engaged in any collaborative
effort; rather it was seeking Mr. Karmel’s termination.

[
60
]

As indicated at the outset of this judgment, the
reasons given for Mr. Karmel’s dismissal were wide ranging. They encompassed
areas that Mr. Karmel was responsible for as school Principal. He reported to
the Board by way of numerous reports. He was part of numerous committees in the
school that dealt with of his areas of responsibility. With these
responsibilities in mind, particularly as they relate to the reasons given for
Mr. Karmel’s termination, I turn to the details of the October 29 letter.

iii.

The October 29 letter and follow-up
correspondence

[
61
]

The letter begins with setting out the
enrollment problem faced by the CJA, which was a significant concern to those
responsible for school governance. Yet the problem was complex, and in order to
deal with it effectively a collaborative approach was required. Mr. Karmel
testified that the enrollment issue was always on his mind and that all of his
decisions reflected his concern about CJA’s enrollment. Indeed, the most
thoughtful views on enrollment in evidence before me were those of Mr. Karmel.
As he said, the issue was entwined with the CJA’s self-perception, and
indicated the need for a strategic plan going forward. Enrollment was also was
tied up with the school’s morale, which was dependent upon good faith
collaboration between the administration and the Board.

[
62
]

One specific example of these issues, as set out
in the evidence of Mr. Karmel and others, was that the CJA had not resolved the
tension between its values of inclusion and the promotion of special
programming for gifted children. Parents of gifted children were constantly
looking for programming that offered their children the best chance to excel
academically. The evidence before me indicates that Mr. Karmel was the only person
who attempted to address this tension, and the only one who had a considered
view on the matter.

[
63
]

Moreover, I have no hesitation in accepting Mr.
Karmel’s evidence that he constantly worked at his PIP with little or no
feedback from the PEC. Yet the PEC’s October 29 letter went on to reference Mr.
Karmel’s PIP and a number of specific problems. The first problem cited was “professionalism.”
Under this heading, the letter referred to communication with parents that
included spelling and grammatical errors. The letter did not offer supporting
examples, and the evidence does not support that this was a serious concern. I
believe that the criticism emanated from an email at Tab 193, to Mr. Kettner
from Ms. Horwitz. She had just heard from another parent who received communication
with spelling errors and typos. The October 29 letter further specified that
administration or staff had been disrespectful to parents. While the record
discloses that there were occasional heated exchanges over some issues, this is,
in my view, typical of any school. It was not something that warranted undue
attention on anyone’s part.

[
64
]

The letter also complained that staff members had
been sending emails on Jewish holidays. Mr. Karmel acknowledged that the policy
was to prevent this from happening, and I accept his evidence. The alleged
failure by Mr. Karmel to reply to email correspondence and meeting requests no
doubt refers to Mr. Kettner’s memo to his fellow committee members at Tab 194
that Mr. Karmel had not responded to his requests. I do not find this to be a
valid ground for termination, as a simple phone call from Mr. Kettner would
have remedied the issue. The final specific example relates to an isolated
incident involving foster children, and the allegation was not borne out in the
evidence before me. I was completely satisfied as to Mr. Karmel’s explanation
on this matter.

[
65
]

In my view, the PEC’s request for a draft action
plan on professionalism was unnecessary because it was not based on meritorious
concerns. Furthermore, the requests for a written weekly report detailing any
lapse in professionalism was an ill-advised request for the reasons set out by
Mr. Karmel in his subsequent communications. As I have already determined, the PEC
was not acting in good faith and was actively seeking Mr. Karmel’s termination.

[
66
]

The complaint related to technology integration
is, in my view, equally lacking in substance. The CJA, like many organizations
in 2012, was attempting to embrace technology and to use it both in the
classroom and for communication with parents. As is often the case with
technology, implementation was a challenge because parents, students and
teachers have different levels of computer skills. Utilization was neither
uniform nor predictable. Furthermore, Mr. Karmel was not an expert in this
field. The person responsible for technology integration, Mr. Suissa, was
involved in presentations to the Board on the subject. Mr. Suissa also sat on
the technology committee, which had regular meetings. In fact, Mr. Kettner was
also a member of that committee. Reports related to technology were often the
subject of Mr. Karmel’s administrative submissions that were given at Board
meetings.

[
67
]

On my review of the evidence, I am satisfied
that the CJA’s technology policy was both sound and necessary. Though it
encountered varied reception, this was dependent upon the computer sophistication
of parents and teachers. I can find no fault with the administration and its
approach to technology integration. Moreover, I believe that Mr. Karmel and
others who were involved in technology integration cooperated fully in delivering
the information that the Board or PEC requested. This was accomplished through
routine reports and specific responses made to the Board and PEC by Mr. Karmel
and Mr. Suissa. I find that Mr. Karmel is not at fault on this issue, and
certainly not to an extent that would warrant cause for termination.

[
68
]

The final allegations in the October 29 letter
are specific to the PIP. As I have stated, Mr. Karmel’s evidence was that he
was following up with respect to each aspect of the plan. I accept that
evidence. Moreover, Tab 144 provides Mr. Karmel’s notes relating to a meeting
held April 5, 2012, with Mr. Kettner. These notes detail the ways in which each
and every item in the PIP was reviewed.

[
69
]

As mentioned above, Mr. Karmel did not receive
any meaningful feedback to the responses given to previous meetings until he
received the October 29 letter. There had been little discussion between the PEC
and Mr. Karmel, despite his attempts to provide meaningful answers the PEC’s
earlier concerns. Furthermore, it is my view that the PEC’s complaints had
little impact, if any, upon the enrollment or the financial dilemmas facing the
CJA. Ironically, the greatest problem facing the CJA during the fall of 2012
was its governance. It had become dysfunctional. The situation, as described by
Ms. Forman at in her March 2012 email at Tab 124, had worsened.

[
70
]

By early November, Mr. Karmel was near his
breaking point. He had been taking medication for sleep and for depression. Nevertheless,
he authored a comprehensive response to the October 29 letter, dated November 2,
which he sent to the PEC. Mr. Karmel acknowledged and replied to the issues
enumerated in the October 29 letter; see Tab 206. He also indicated that he
expected a reply to his correspondence. Furthermore, he said it was his
expectation that the Board Chair would distribute his correspondence to all
Board members. He went on to request that he be advised if that was not the
case. There is no evidence before me, or in Mr. Kettner’s reply, to determine whether
Mr. Kettner’s correspondence was distributed to the Board.

[
71
]

Mr. Karmel’s letter went on to respond to the
issues raised in the October 29 letter. Mr. Karmel made the point that, in
addition to his onerous responsibilities as Principal, the letter demanded that
he write additional reports. His response was that he would update the Board and
the PEC as to operational matters of the school.  He pointed out that he had
already addressed all the concerns raised by the PEC in previous
correspondence. He stated that if there were any questions he would be pleased
to set aside time to meet and discuss them. He reiterated his belief that “the
way forward is true dialogue and mutual good faith.” In the next paragraph he
stated  that “given the above and this turn of events, let’s meet and discuss
in good faith and I am sure we can continue to find far more common ground than
a culture of differences.”

[
72
]

I have found myself asking numerous times why the
PEC did not meet with Mr. Karmel for a candid exchange of views. The answer can
only be that Mr. Kettner consciously decided against it. I find this to be
astonishing, yet I received no credible explanation as to why none of Mr.
Karmel’s invitations to meet were accepted.

[
73
]

I can only conclude that the paint incident of
August 16, 2011, soured Mr. Kettner on Mr. Karmel as Principal. Following the
meeting with Mr. Karmel and Ms. Horwitz on August 17, 2011, Mr. Kettner felt
that Mr. Karmel was going to make things difficult for him. He felt Mr. Karmel was
going to be “resistant”. The speaking notes at Tab 283 for the October 2011 “in
camera” meeting confirm this finding:

Ben
doesn’t think we’re entitled to manage him--- I with the consent of the special
committee need to be able to manage him if he needs managing. Right now--- he
needs managing. He doesn’t respect any sort of authority from me at this
moment.--- If we continue to allow him free rein it will be seen in the eyes of
the law as consent to his behavior we’ll have very little power to control him
in the future.

[
74
]

Mr. Kettner saw Mr. Karmel as a threat to his
authority, and he was determined to either bring Mr. Karmel around to his own
way of thinking, or get rid of him. It was early in the 2011-2012 school year
that Mr. Kettner sought legal counsel.

[
75
]

Mr. Kettner did not take criticism lightly. When
Mr. Karmel challenged some of Mr. Kettner’s governance methods and his lack of
transparency, he got angry. Mr. Kettner did not like the Ambassador Program
because he was concerned it would turn into a “parking lot mafia”.  Disgruntled
parents could make trouble for the executive, and he absolutely did not agree
with Mr. Karmel that the school should facilitate constructive criticism. Any
criticism received by Mr. Kettner from parents, particularly Board parents, he
saw as a criticism of Mr. Karmel. But Mr. Karmel was not a “yes” man, and his
standing up to parents was seen by Mr. Kettner as insensitive and arrogant.

[
76
]

Mr. Kettner, in his emails and during his
evidence, said he was doing everything to help Mr. Karmel succeed. For example,
in Tab 124, his March 1, 2012 email to Ms. Forman stated, “there is nothing
more than I want to see Ben triumph.” That statement is not credible. Seen in
the context of all of the other emails, it is clear that Mr. Kettner had formed
the opinion that Mr. Karmel was not the Principal that he wanted for the CJA.
Mr. Kettner wanted things done his way. The rest of the email to Ms. Forman is
a rant, or, as Ms. Forman referred to it, “Ben bashing”. I believe that Mr.
Kettner took every opportunity to persuade his colleagues on the Board that Mr.
Karmel was a hopeless Principal.

[
77
]

His memos, speaking notes, and the other
evidence make it clear that Mr. Kettner was not working to help Mr. Karmel
succeed. Rather he took every opportunity to sabotage Mr. Karmel in the minds
of his colleagues on the PEC and on the Board. He excluded Mr. Karmel from the
Board orientation meeting in the fall of 2012, and from an initial meeting to discuss
the CJA’s strategic plan in December 2012. Mr. Karmel was not informed about
the meetings, nor did he receive a copy of the minutes or the documents related
to it. While unfair and regrettable, this is not surprising considering Mr.
Kettner’s intention to oust Mr. Karmel as Principal.

[
78
]

The PEC members maintained the position that Mr.
Karmel’s November 2 letter was “non-responsive,” and did not constitute the
reports requested in their October 29 letter. I disagree. However, anyone
reading the correspondence between Mr. Karmel and the PEC can plainly see that
they were communicating at cross-purposes. They did not see eye to eye on
important governance issues, and they had very different views on what
constituted collaboration between a Principal and a school board. The situation
cried out for a meeting, yet what ensued was another demand letter from the PEC
dated November 11, 2012, at Tab 209. Rather than accepting Mr. Karmel’s
invitation to meet, the letter reiterated that the Board’s responsibility for overseeing
the operation of the school, and as part of that “we oversee and manage you as
the school Principal. You report and answer to the Board.”

[
79
]

The November 11 letter was a continuation of the
determined effort by Mr. Kettner to get rid of Mr. Karmel. He defends the areas
identified in the October 29 letter as priorities necessary to address the
CJA’s falling enrollment and financial troubles.  In my view, blaming the CJA’s
struggles on the issue listed in the October 29 letter was an unreasonable assessment.
Mr. Kettner went on to say in the November 11 letter that

the
items and deadlines were made with the careful consideration as to what is
important and for the success of the school in providing the best possible
outcomes for the students while at the same time taking into account your busy
schedule.

Again,
it is my view that this conclusion was not one that would have been reached by
a reasonable, fully informed Board member.

[
80
]

At least by this point in the narrative the die
is cast. Subsequent correspondence contained repeated and additional demands by
Mr. Kettner. These are met by increasingly frustrated responses by Mr. Karmel.
For example, Mr. Kettner complains at Tab 13 about Mr. Karmel leaving a meeting
at 9:20 pm and takes great exception to that. Mr. Karmel in subsequent
correspondence and in his evidence responds to this and I am satisfied with his
response. Nevertheless, it does not really matter. The parties were not
effectively communicating if they ever did. The story only has one ending; that
is Mr. Karmel’s termination.

[
81
]

Parents of students including board parents were
complaining about the grade four class. In December, Mr. Kettner demanded an immediate
report from Mr. Karmel by December 14. Mr. Karmel was frustrated because he did
not think that the evidence supported the parents’ complaints. Notwithstanding
his frustration, he did respond on December 10 (Tab 223) and the substance of
the response is on pages 4 and 5. However, by this time the relationship is dysfunctional.
There is little mutual respect and Mr. Kettner is determined to terminate Mr.
Karmel.

iv.

Conclusion on the evidence

[
82
]

There is little point in setting out the rest of
the correspondence. By the end of 2012, as I have emphasized, the die was cast.
By the time the special meeting of the Board was called in February 2013, it
was obvious that the PEC would recommend Mr. Karmel’s removal. Since Mr.
Kettner was in control of the flow of information, no one on the Board could
meaningfully question the recommendation. It was clear to all Board members
that the relationship between Mr. Karmel and Mr. Kettner had become intolerable
and was not sustainable. The Board had long since determined that it would
stand behind Mr. Kettner.

[
83
]

Once the PEC delivered the October 29 letter, it
ignored Mr. Karmel’s responses or deemed them “non-responsive.” Either the
members of the PEC did not read the materials available to them, or they were
deaf to Mr. Karmel’s point of view. They made little or no effort to learn Mr.
Karmel’s opinion on any of the issues. Remarkably, in my view, both Mr. Brener
and Ms. Eisenberg found a number of Mr. Karmel’s emails bordering on insubordination
or condescension. In one case, Mr. Brener found Mr. Karmel’s email at Tab 71,
and in particular, the third paragraph on page 6 to be “a pre-emptive strike at
an allegation of constructive dismissal.” That suggestion is not credible. Mr.
Karmel’s dedication to the CJA was common knowledge, and the success of the school
was of the upmost importance to him. In my view, outside of his family and his faith,
the CJA was the most important thing in Mr. Karmel’s life.

[
84
]

Further, the tight-knit nature of the Calgary
Jewish community meant that the issues faced by Mr. Karmel in his role as
Principal of the CJA were especially significant. While some professionals
distinguish between their work and personal lives, Mr. Karmel’s were one in the
same. His future at the CJA was therefore bound up with his role and reputation
in his community.

[
85
]

The members of the Board who testified on behalf
of the CJA stressed that they considered one of Mr. Karmel’s biggest failings
to be budgetary choice he made with regard to the Gain Program. This program was
aimed at gifted children and children with identified needs. The CJA hired Ms.
Kristen Walker as the Gain Program Coordinator but she was only able to work
part-time. Because she was the only person qualified to do the job (and Mr. Karmel
said she was very qualified), the CJA left several thousands of dollars earmarked
for the Gain Program unspent. I am completely satisfied with Mr. Karmel’s
explanation on this subject. It was impossible to get a qualified person full-time,
and the CJA paid Ms. Walker a part-time salary. It would have made no sense to
spend the money simply because it had been earmarked in the budget. I therefore
do not accept the evidence regarding the Gain Program as a valid criticism of
Mr. Karmel.

[
86
]

As I have previously stated, Mr. Kettner clearly
recruited members of the PEC to take a certain view of Mr. Karmel. The rest of
the Board was faced with the unanimous recommendation of the PEC, which the
Board itself had mandated to monitor and manage Mr. Karmel. I find that the PEC
made no effort to conduct a fair investigation of the issues. At no time was
Mr. Karmel’s position adequately put forward to the Board.

[
87
]

Mr. Karmel was terminated by the Board on
February 25, 2013. The reasons for termination have, on the evidence before me,
no merit. I have carefully reviewed all the evidence and in my view, no person
fully informed, could come to the conclusion that the CJA had just cause to
dismiss Mr. Karmel. Far from being wilfully disobedient, Mr. Karmel made numerous
good faith attempts to resolve the issues that plagued the CJA’s governance.
Unfortunately, and through no fault of his own, individuals who sought his
termination rejected his efforts.

[
88
]

I have re-listened to much of the testimony and
have reviewed my notes, all the memoranda, correspondence and emails entered as
exhibits. I accept Mr. Karmel’s explanation with the respect to each of the
reasons for termination set out in the termination letter. I find that Mr.
Karmel was not guilty of wilfully disregarding reasonable demands by the Board
or the PEC. Mr. Kettner was pursuing a strategy of papering a path to Mr.
Karmel’s termination in such a way as to spare the CJA from paying the balance
of Mr. Karmel’s salary under the remaining term of his contact. This was a
wrongful dismissal carried out in bad faith. Mr. Karmel is therefore entitled
to damages.

Damages

[
89
]

Mr. Karmel is entitled to damages for the salary
owed to him under the employment contract, as well as aggravated damages in
compensation for the bad faith conduct of Mr. Kettner and the PEC acting in
their official capacities on behalf of the CJA. I turn first to the employment
contract.

[
90
]

The parties agreed that the outstanding balance
owed under the contract is as follows: $606,027.97 for base salary; $39,391.85
for the lost benefit of RRSP matching contributions; and $24,568.24 for loss of
the group benefit plan. Damages under the employment contract therefore total
$669,988.06.

[
91
]

Mr. Karmel is also entitled to aggravated
damages. It has long been established that employers owe a duty of good faith
and fair dealing when terminating an employee. The breach of this duty is
compensable with aggravated “bad faith”, “
Wallace
” or “
Honda
”
damages, in addition to damages for wrongful dismissal: see
Wallace v
United Grain Growers
,
1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 SCR 701, SCJ No 94,
Keays v Honda
Canada Inc
,
2008 SCC 39
, [2008] 2 SCR 362.

[
92
]

The law requires employers to be “candid,
reasonable, honest and forthright with their employees.” Employers cannot
lawfully engage “in conduct that is unfair or is in bad faith by being, for
example, untruthful, misleading or unduly insensitive” see
Wallace

at
para
98
.

[
93
]

My reasons articulated in this judgment make
clear that  Mr. Kettner, acting in his official capacity on behalf of the CJA, was
in violation of the duties enumerated in
Wallace
. The other
members of the PEC acquiesced. Not only was the PEC unreasonable in recommending
the termination of Mr. Karmel’s contract, it also acted in bad faith for much
of the time leading up to the termination.

[
94
]

Two recent cases of the Supreme Court of Canada
are directly relevant here. First, in
Bhasin v Hrynew
,
2014 SCC
71
, the Court was unanimous in recognizing that “good faith contractual
performance is a general organizing principle of the common law,” see para 33. As
a result of the decision in
Bhasin
, parties to a contract have a
duty to act honestly in the performance of their contractual obligations.

[
95
]

While
Bhasin
was not specific to
the employment context, the Supreme Court’s decision in

Potter v New
Brunswick Legal Aid Services Commission
,
2015 SCC 10
,  referenced the
good faith requirements in
Bhasin

in the context of wrongful
dismissal. The Court defined the employer’s duty of good faith as one which
extends throughout the duration of employment, and not just at the time or
event of termination. Employers must therefore demonstrate good faith for the
entirety of the employment contract.

[
96
]

In the matter before me, it is clear that the
CJA failed in its duty to act in good faith for a period of about 18 months.

[
97
]

An award of  $200,000 for aggravated damages was
recently upheld by the Ontario Court of Appeal in the wrongful dismissal
context in
Boucher v Wal-Mart Canada Corp
,
2014 ONCA 419
, [2014]
OJ No 2452. In affirming the quantum of the award, Justice Laskin stated at
para 66 that

[a]ggravated damages are compensatory
damages. They are part of breach of contract damages. They compensate a plaintiff
for the additional harm suffered because of the way the contract was breached.
In a wrongful dismissal claim, aggravated damages may be awarded against the
employer where "the employer engages in conduct during the course of
dismissal that is 'unfair or is in bad faith'... However, ‘the normal distress
and hurt feelings resulting from dismissal are not compensable.’

[
98
]

The evidence of Ms. Karmel was that Mr. Karmel
suffered considerably before, during and after his sudden termination mid-year.
Rumors were rampant surrounding his firing. He felt isolated. He and his family
felt socially uncomfortable in their otherwise tight knit community. Although Mr.
Karmel diligently sought similar employment, he met with no success. Eventually
he retrained and became a licensed private investigator.

[
99
]

I am satisfied that Mr. Karmel has proven intentional
and calculated actions by those acting on behalf of the CJA, which resulted in
his mental distress and isolation in his community. Not only were these actions
carried out in the course of Mr. Karmel’s termination, they also persisted for
months prior.

[
100
]

The case before me was not one of “normal
distress and hurt feelings.” Rather the CJA’s conduct was consistent with the sort
of bad faith dealings that aggravated damages are intended to remedy. Indeed,
the facts of the case are particularly insidious. I therefore award Mr. Karmel
$200,000.00 in aggravated damages for the harm he suffered because of the CJA’s
conduct. While this amount is at the high end of the spectrum for bad faith
damages, the harm to Mr. Karmel’s reputation and mental health warrants a
significant compensatory award.

[
101
]

I have not examined the issue of whether defamation
has been established in this case. I do not find defamation to be necessary. Nor
does it fit comfortably with an analysis of wrongful termination. As my reasons
make clear, aggravated damages provide sufficient compensation for the harm
suffered by Mr. Karmel.

[
102
]

I note that while the conduct may well have been
sufficiently egregious as to warrant punitive damages, I have awarded an amount
to compensate Mr. Karmel. I do not believe that he would wish to punish the CJA
with further punitive damages.

[
103
]

The Plaintiff shall have interest in accordance
with the Judgment Interest Act. The parties may speak to costs if they cannot
agree.
